title: How do you handle exceptions globally in ASP.NET Core?
description: Exception handler middleware, IExceptionHandler, ProblemDetails (RFC 7807), and logging without leaking internals.

data.text: **Question:** How do you handle exceptions globally in ASP.NET Core?

Register an exception-handling layer early in the pipeline: `UseExceptionHandler()` with a re-execution path (or .NET 7+ `AddExceptionHandler<IExceptionHandler>()`), and return a standardized **ProblemDetails** (RFC 7807) response with the right status code, a correlation id, and **no stack trace in production**. Keep `try/catch` in actions for business-level recovery (compensation, alternate flows); use the global handler as the safety net that converts unexpected exceptions into a consistent 500 body — plus structured logging for diagnosis.

**Layers, from action to pipeline:**
- **Action-level try/catch** — expected failures you can *handle*: validation, fallback, cancellation. Rethrow what you can't handle
- **Filters** — `IExceptionFilter`/`IAsyncExceptionFilter` see MVC-handled exceptions (legacy but useful for controller-wide mapping)
- **Exception handler middleware** — the global safety net: catches anything unhandled, re-executes an error path (`/error`) or invokes registered `IExceptionHandler`s
- **Developer exception page** — verbose HTML/stack traces; Development environment only (`UseDeveloperExceptionPage` is wired by default in dev)
- **BadHttpRequestException / body-read failures** — occur before actions; the handler middleware still catches them

**Returning ProblemDetails:**
- Content type `application/problem+json`, fields: `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`, `traceId`
- Map exception types to status codes: domain `NotFoundException` → 404, `ConflictException` → 409, unknown → 500 with generic detail
- ASP.NET Core auto-populates `traceId` (and `errors` for validation via `ValidationProblem`)
- In production `detail` must be generic — exception messages can leak SQL, paths, internals; log the full exception server-side instead
- Multiple exception handlers can be registered; each decides `CanHandle`

**Cross-cutting:**
- Structured logging at the boundary: one log entry per failure with exception, request path, user, correlation id
- Distributed tracing: attach `Activity`/trace id to the response so support can correlate client reports
- Cancellation (`OperationCanceledException` when the client disconnected) should **not** be logged as a server error

data.title: Global handler returning ProblemDetails

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Layered thinking: handle expected failures locally, unexpected ones globally
- Knowledge of ProblemDetails and correct status-code mapping
- Security awareness: no stack traces or exception messages to clients in production
- Practical logging: correlation ids, not swallowing exceptions silently

items: catch (Exception) { } with no rethrow — the request 'succeeds' with corrupt state
Returning 200 with an error message in the body — clients can't branch on status
Developer exception page (or full exception detail) left on in production
Middleware order mistakes: exception handler registered after components that can throw past it
Logging every OperationCanceledException as an error — client disconnects are noise
One giant catch-all that maps everything to 500, losing 404/409 semantics
What is the difference between UseExceptionHandler with a path and IExceptionHandler?
How do you keep error responses consistent across 20 microservices?
Where does UseDeveloperExceptionPage belong, and how does it stay out of production?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: try/catch for expected, recoverable failures; global handler as safety net
Return application/problem+json with accurate status codes and traceId
Generic details to clients, full exceptions to logs/traces
Order the handler early; Development-only verbosity
data.takeaway: One global layer converts every unexpected failure into a consistent, safe ProblemDetails response — while logs and trace ids keep it diagnosable.
